CANDY KLONDIKE.

A candy Klondike has been discovered at Hither-green, Lewisham, and hundreds of children have not only prospected and dug, but have actually found sweetmeat treasures in the soil. The reopening of the London County Council schools has interfered somewhat with mining operations, but the youngsters worked late last night to make up for lost time.

The magic region is a sand-heap on land on which Councillor J. Stanford is building a row of houses. Lewisham children have dug holes and built hillocks there throughout the summer, and until Friday last nothing better had been found than an occasional battered tin, but early on that day a small boy discovered a carefully tied packet buried in the sand. It contained chocolate creams!
The news spread like wildfire, and presently there was a scramble of young prospectors with wooden spades, trowels, pokers, pieces of zinc, and, when tools lacked, ten fingers each.

One little girl, working with her mother's fire shovel, dug up twenty-two packets, all nicely fastened, and containing chocolate creams, Turkish delight, acid tablets, chewing gum, and pineapple drops.
NO BLANKS.
She leads the party in the amount of treasure unearthed, but none fail utterly, and every time a packet is found a shriek of joy goes up, and work in the neighbourhood takes on renewed activity.

The children were far too busy at first to inquire into the mystery of this buried treasure, but it has been learned by the non-mining population that Mr. Stanford, who is a member of the school committee, wanted the treat for the little ones.

The stock of a sweetmeat shop came into his possession in the course of business, and it occurred to him that burial in the sand, where children would be sure to find it, would be the best disposition he could make or it. So, with the assistance of four men and his family, the sweets were tied up in 250 packets and buried early in the school. The children arrived.

Miss Dora JunenWheeler, nineteen year old high school girl of Hollis, L.I., now on duty as swimming instructor and life guard at Ocean Beach, Fire Island, L.I.

She rescued a man at Ocean Beach about two years ago and her deed brought her considerable redemption. She was rewarded with a costly watch, a handsome ring, a medal and a gift of gold.

JUNE 1.—The poppies give us some of our most brilliant summer flowers. To-day the fine Oriental poppies begin to open their blossoms. There are now many beautiful varieties in exquisite shades of colour. These poppies last well in water if cut when the buds have just burst.

The dainty Iceland poppies—good subjects for the rockery—also open to-day, while the single and double Welsh poppies (Cambrica) make quite a gay show on a dry bank. For cutting, papaver pilosum (orange-buff) is always in demand.
